meta.title: 15-Day Strategic Plan — Educative + NeetCode
meta.subtitle: Strategic, not exhaustive. Highest-value patterns + core system design across 15 days.
meta.split: ~2 hrs coding + ~1.5 hrs system design + log
sources: Grokking the Modern System Design Interview (Educative)

rules.title: No AI, no autocomplete, no copilot — for all 10 days of practice.
rules.body: Plain editor or the LeetCode box. Type every character yourself. This feels awful for 2 days, then your recall comes back. The discomfort IS the muscle rebuilding.

rules.title: The 5-minute think rule.
rules.body: Before writing any code, spend 5 minutes restating the problem, an example, and your approach out loud. Coding before you have a plan is what causes freezing.

rules.title: The re-solve rule (most important).
rules.body: If stuck 25–30 min, read the solution — then CLOSE it and re-solve from a blank screen. Reading solutions feels productive but builds nothing. Re-solving from blank rebuilds recall.

rules.title: Talk while you code.
rules.body: Narrate your thinking out loud, even alone. Interviews are spoken — you must practice coding and explaining at the same time. This also fixes the 'mind wandering' problem.

rules.title: One pattern at a time.
rules.body: Don't jump around. Finish a pattern's problems before the next. Jumping around is how you feel busy but retain nothing.

rules.title: Track a tiny log.
rules.body: Each day write: problems solved, which I failed, which pattern. Re-attempt failed ones 2 days later. This single habit beats doing 2× the volume.

rules.title: Stop on time. Sleep.
rules.body: A tired brain doesn't encode memory. 4–6 focused hours beats 9 scattered ones. Protect sleep — it's when the learning consolidates.

dailyStructure.body: Warm up by re-solving 1 problem from yesterday (builds confidence), then 4–6 new problems on the day's pattern. Easy first, then medium.
Learn the day's concept (read + take notes in your own words), then connect it to PRISM/Tempo — 'where did I use this in real life?'
Update your log — solved / failed / pattern. Note one thing that clicked and one that didn't.

days.title: Two Pointers

items.label: Getting Ready for the System Design Interview
Log: solved / failed / pattern. One thing that clicked + one that didn't.

days.successCheck: Momentum day. You can state in one sentence WHEN to use two pointers.

days.title: Fast & Slow Pointers

items.label: Read 'Introduction to Fast and Slow Pointers'
Preliminary System Design Concepts (network abstraction, consistency, failure models — all 4 lessons)
Re-solve one Day 1 problem from blank. Log it.

days.successCheck: Cycle detection feels automatic. Draw the pointers before coding.

days.title: Sliding Window

items.label: Work the easy/medium window problems in the chapter
Re-type the core template from blank
Availability, reliability, scalability, fault tolerance (work the 7 lessons)
Log. Re-solve a Day 2 failure from blank.

days.successCheck: You can explain sliding window vs two pointers.

days.title: Stacks + In-Place Linked List

blocks.title: Grokking · In-Place Manipulation of a Linked List

items.label: Reverse a sublist — re-type from blank

blocks.title: Grokking SD · Back-of-Envelope + Building Blocks intro

days.successCheck: Reversing a list and matching-pairs problems are automatic.

items.label: Re-type the template from blank — watch left<=right and mid
Load Balancers (3 lessons: placement, algorithms, tiers)
Log. Re-solve a binary search problem from blank.

days.title: Tree DFS

items.label: Memorize template: base case → recurse → combine
Databases chapter (5 lessons: types, replication, partitioning, trade-offs)

days.successCheck: You can write a DFS template from memory.

days.title: Tree BFS

items.label: Re-solve Level Order from blank. Log.

days.successCheck: BFS via queue is automatic. Half the patterns done.

days.title: Top K Elements + Two Heaps

items.label: Log. Heap = priority queue; 'top K / Kth' → heap.

days.successCheck: You reach for a heap on 'top K' without thinking.

days.title: Intervals + K-way Merge

items.label: Log. Intervals → sort by start, then merge.

days.successCheck: Interval problems have a clear template now.

days.title: Hash Maps + Knowing What to Track

items.label: Rate Limiter chapter (5 lessons: algorithms, traffic management)

days.title: RESHADED + first case study

blocks.title: Grokking SD · Concluding Building Blocks + RESHADED

items.label: Concluding the Building Blocks Discussion (4 lessons)
2 mixed medium problems from any learned pattern, timed 30 min each, no AI
Log. Say the RESHADED steps out loud.

days.successCheck: You can recite RESHADED and applied it to one real design.

days.title: Subsets + Backtracking

items.label: Word Search or Combination Sum (one problem)
Design Twitter — full walkthrough (caching, storage, fan-out)
Log. Backtracking is just controlled DFS with undo.

days.successCheck: You understand the subsets/backtracking template shape.

days.title: Dynamic Programming (1D) + Graphs intro

items.label: Climbing Stairs / House Robber (1D memo shape only — don't rabbit-hole)

blocks.title: Grokking SD · Design a Newsfeed System

items.label: Log. DP = remember subproblem answers. Don't over-study it.

days.successCheck: You recognize the 1D-DP shape and can traverse a graph.

days.title: Timed simulation + mock

items.label: 4 random medium problems across learned patterns, 30 min each, TIMED, no AI, narrate out loud
Use Educative's AI Mock Interview for one coding round

blocks.title: Grokking SD · Design Uber OR WhatsApp + AI Mock

items.label: One more case study (Uber or WhatsApp)
Educative AI Mock Interview — one system design round, out loud
Log which patterns you spotted fast vs froze on.

days.successCheck: Pressure rep done. ~50+ problems solved across the plan. That's your proof.

days.title: Light review + rest — DO NOT CRAM

items.label: Re-solve 5 previously-failed problems from blank. Smooth = ready.
Skim the pattern list — don't grind
Re-read RESHADED + your strongest case study once
Design 'a content management + delivery platform' out loud (this is Tempo/PRISM — your home turf)
Prepare 2–3 questions to ask interviewers. Sleep early.

days.successCheck: Arrive calm and confident. No new material today.

framework.title: The 6-Step System Design Framework
framework.tagline: Use this exact order on EVERY design question. The order itself stops you from wandering — same fix as behavioural answers.

steps.title: Clarify requirements (3–5 min)
steps.body: Functional (what it does) + non-functional (scale, latency, consistency). Ask: how many users? reads vs writes? Don't design until you know the scale. Interviewers WANT you to ask.

steps.title: Estimate scale
steps.body: Rough numbers — QPS, storage, read/write ratio. Even ballpark shows you think about scale. Recipe: DAU × actions/day ÷ 86,400 = avg QPS, × 3 for peak, × bytes for storage.

steps.title: Define the API
steps.body: A few key endpoints with inputs/outputs. This grounds everything that follows.

steps.title: High-level design
steps.body: Draw the boxes: client → load balancer → service(s) → cache → database → queue. Talk through one request's path end to end.

steps.title: Deep-dive 1–2 components
steps.body: Pick the interesting parts — the data model, the caching strategy, how you keep things in sync. THIS is where your PRISM / outbox / partitioning knowledge shines. Steer toward what you've operated.

steps.title: Address bottlenecks & tradeoffs
steps.body: Where does it break at scale? Consistency vs availability? Single points of failure? Naming tradeoffs out loud is what separates senior from junior.

framework.advantage: PRISM and Tempo are a real distributed system you built — a CMS with authoring/delivery split, caching tiers, a transactional outbox, partitioned databases, and multi-region deployment. Most candidates invent these from theory. You can speak from having operated them. In the deep-dive step, steer toward what you know.
